newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden raises human rights with China but no threats.
newsitem.headline: Sweden raises human rights with China but no threats.

text.p: Sweden raised concerns over China's human rights abuses with visiting Vice-Premier Wu Bangguo on Friday and stood firmly by a Danish proposal to the U.N. Human Rights Commission condemning such violations.

Denmark has sponsored a censure motion against China at the commission in Geneva next week and is trying, aided by the United States, to lift the number of co-sponsors to 30 from 15. China says economic links with supporters of the motion could suffer.
Swedish ambassador Lars Danielsson told Reuters that Prime Minister Goran Persson conveyed his nation's concerns to Wu, in Sweden for a five-day visit.
"The human rights issue was the most important theme of their discussions," said Danielsson, who monitored the meeting.
"But the talks were friendly with no warnings given."
U.N. Human Rights Commission members have complained of being subjected to a fierce campaign by Beijing, alleging trade and other pressures are piling up.
Many diplomats expect China to escape censure for the seventh year running when the main United Nations rights body votes on Tuesday.

Danielsson said there was no pressure in the meeting with Persson. The Swedish prime minister came under fire at home last year, facing an unsuccessful vote of no confidence, after allegedly complimenting China's political stability during a visit.
"But China knows we are not now a member of the U.N. Human Rights Commission so we are not in the same position as Denmark," he said.
"There were discussions about the possibility of further economic relations between Stockholm and China."

Wu arrived in Stockholm early on Friday from Finland and was to meet a number of Swedish companies including telecommunications firm Ericsson, household retailer IKEA, vehicle maker AB Volvo and toolmaker SKF.

"Even though this is an industrial trip, representatives from the Swedish government will bring up the matter of human rights which is a standing point on the agenda when we meet China," Foreign Ministry spokesman Staffan Bjorck said.
On Monday Wu, one of China's six deputy premiers, meet King Carl Gustaf.
Representatives from human rights groups in Sweden sent letters of protest about China to the Swedish government and were organising a protest march on Monday.

The general secretary of Swedish Amnesty, Anita Klum, said campaigners did not object to economic ties between the two countries but were concerned about human rights abuses, particularly the condition of childrens' homes in China.
"I think we should use all the chances we have to bring these issues up," Klum told Reuters.
Ever since the 1989 crackdown in Tiananmen Square, Western countries have tried to get the U.N. body to at least debate allegations of executions and torture in China.
Last year, 27 states voted in favour of China's no-action motion, 20 voted against with six abstentions.
